details:
**Brexit**
Johnson was the most prominent face of the 2016 Leave campaign. He became Prime Minister on a promise to "get Brexit done," and the United Kingdom formally left the European Union on January 31, 2020, under his government.

**Succeeding Theresa May**
Johnson replaced Theresa May as Conservative leader and Prime Minister in July 2019, after attacking her Brexit withdrawal plan as too soft. He served as Prime Minister until 2022.

**Mayor of London**
Johnson served two terms as Mayor of London from 2008 to 2016, a period that included the 2012 London Olympics. It is a common giveaway, usually paired with "Prime Minister."

**Michael Gove**
A fellow Conservative and Leave campaigner who was Johnson's ally and rival. In 2016 Gove withdrew his support and ran against him for party leader, effectively ending Johnson's first leadership bid; in the 2019 contest, Johnson's supporters were accused of tactically lending votes to Jeremy Hunt to knock Gove out of the final round.

**Foreign Secretary under Theresa May**
Johnson was Foreign Secretary from 2016 to 2018, before resigning in protest over May's "Chequers" Brexit plan. His tenure was marked by repeated gaffes.

**Prorogation of Parliament (2019)**
In August 2019, Johnson advised the Queen to prorogue (suspend) Parliament for five weeks, limiting MPs' ability to block a no-deal Brexit. The UK Supreme Court unanimously ruled the prorogation unlawful in September 2019.

**Dominic Cummings and Sajid Javid's resignation**
Dominic Cummings was Johnson's powerful chief adviser and the mastermind of the Vote Leave campaign. In February 2020, Chancellor Sajid Javid resigned after being told to fire his own advisers, a dispute widely blamed on Cummings.

**"Boris bikes"**
The nickname for London's public bicycle hire scheme, launched in 2010 while Johnson was mayor. It was later sponsored by Santander and is officially called Santander Cycles.

**Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe**
A British-Iranian woman detained in Iran from 2016 on espionage-related charges. As Foreign Secretary, Johnson wrongly told Parliament in 2017 that she had been "teaching people journalism," a claim Iranian authorities cited as grounds for extending her sentence; she was finally released in 2022.

**Kipling at the Shwedagon Pagoda**
On a 2017 visit to Myanmar as Foreign Secretary, Johnson began reciting Rudyard Kipling's colonial-era poem "The Road to Mandalay" inside the sacred Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon. The British ambassador, Andrew Patrick, stopped him by telling him it was "not appropriate."

**COVID-19 diagnosis**
Johnson tested positive for COVID-19 in March 2020, becoming the first major world leader known to have the disease. In April 2020 he was hospitalized and spent several nights in intensive care.

**Daily Telegraph correspondent in Brussels**
Before entering politics, Johnson was the Brussels-based European Community correspondent for The Daily Telegraph from 1989 to 1994. His often exaggerated stories mocking EU regulations helped fuel British Euroscepticism.

**"Great supine protoplasmic invertebrate jellies"**
One of Johnson's colorful insults, used against members of an assembly that had voted against him. It is typical of the flamboyant language for which he is known.

**Alexander Boris de Pfeffel Johnson**
Johnson's full name; he is often nicknamed "BoJo." Questions sometimes accept the full name as an answer.
